newsitem.title: USA: US Congress may review San Antonio Fed cash levels.
newsitem.headline: US Congress may review San Antonio Fed cash levels.

text.p: The U.S. House Banking Committee may hold hearings to look into a mysterious build-up of $3 billion of cash at the Dallas Federal Reserve Bank's San Antonio branch, committee chairman Jim Leach said Tuesday.
Ranking Democrat Henry Gonzalez charged in a letter to Leach last week that the surplus could indicate money laundering activity and called for hearings.

"Committee staff has been instructed to discuss with your staff possible hearings, at both the full committee and subcommittee levels," Leach said in a letter to Gonzalez dated Jan 13 and released on Tuesday.
A cash surplus occurs when the Fed takes in more currency from its member institutions than it issues to meet their demands.
Gonzalez of Texas said he has been unable to determine the source of a "startling increase" in excess cash at the San Antonio branch.

"Only a few Reserve Banks report a currency surplus and many law enforcement sources believe that such surpluses are in large part the result of money laundering," he said. Gonzalez added he had no evidence suggesting criminal activity by any banks.

In his response, Leach said the hearings would examine the extent of money laundering in the Southwest and other areas of the country, how existing anti-laundering laws are being implemented and whether additional laws are needed.

"Money laundering appears to be on the rise," Leach said. "While the American banking system is relatively free from corruption, banks in other parts of the world, from Central America to Russia, are increasingly becoming beltways for money laundering rather than recycling institutions for traditional deposits and loans provided."
Gonzalez said he had asked the Internal Revenue Service and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, or FinCEN, about the cash at the San Antonio branch.
FinCEN could not explain the surplus and reported that the cash build-up was not correlated with banks in the area filing reports of large currency transactions or suspicious activity, Gonzalez said.
The IRS told the congressman in a letter that it did not have authority to look into the matter.
Jim Stull, Fed senior vice president in charge of the San Antonio branch, said in a telephone interview that non-criminal factors likely caused most of the surplus.
"There is a lot of tourism here and in Mexico," Stull said. "Dollars flow into Mexico and have to come back. We think they flow through the border banks.
Further, cash arriving at the San Antonio branch has already been transferred several times among banks, Stull said. "If there's any criminal activity going on, it isn't here," he said.

The branch is conducting a study that could be completed in a month or so to determine the origins of the surplus, Stull added. The study will document the level of legitimate uses causing the cash to build up.
